new_statements.translation: 3.6.1. Unlike tone, intensity stress (sound amplitude measured in decibels) has no distinctive function in Ye'pâ-masa. The placement of primary stress depends largely on the emphasis situation. [...] There is a certain tendency to place intensity stress every two moras, with much individual variation according to emphasis [p. 63] || There are two tonic melodies associated with lexemes: the high or register melody, and the rising or contour melody. A third melody, the low melody, is phonologically atonic and characterizes suffixes and dependent words. [p. 15]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a Tucano record with an empty rule and no statements; Ramirez supplies the type: lexical tone (two tonic melodies vs atonic), with intensity stress explicitly non-distinctive and emphasis-driven.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tucano (Ye'pâ-masa) is a tone language: every lexeme is bimoraic and carries one of two tonic melodies (high/register, written with circumflex on the 2nd mora, or rising/contour, written with acute) or the atonic low melody (suffixes, dependent words); a rising melody's contour tone shifts onto a following non-laryngealized suffix (§3.4.7). Intensity stress is not distinctive: primary stress placement varies with emphasis (u͂yû ['u͂ȷ͂u͂] ~ [u͂'ȷ͂u͂]), with only a tendency to alternate every two moras. Tonal downdrift is the rule (§3.6.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only a tendency to place intensity stress every two moras, with much individual variation by emphasis (p. 63, example da'da+bãsí-bı͂ 'he knows how to work'); no fixed secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: About a dozen lexemes with a falling melody [´ `] (§3.4.4, p. 50); some tonally unstable lexemes whose melody changes with morphological context (§3.4.5); laryngealized suffixes block tone shift (§3.4.9); irregular suffixes and dependent words listed in §15.6.
new_statements.identity_note: West & Welch 1967 describe the Acaricuara dialect (Paca River, Papurí basin, Colombia; data 1963-64) and note unhandled vowel changes in the 'downriver dialect'. Ramirez 1997 describes Ye'pâ-masa, the Tukano of the Brazilian Uaupés (Salesian mission area; fieldwork 1994-96). Both are Tucano proper (tuca1252). The archive.org item listed for Longacre & Woods 1976 is a Cuiva (cui, Guahiban) excerpt, not Tucano.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tucano (Acaricuara dialect) has three contrastive pitch levels (high, mid, low) with lexical pitch patterns (minimal pairs díbá 'poison' vs dìbà 'they are', p. 19). Stress is treated as a suprasegmental phoneme alongside pitch and nasalization: monosyllables are stressed; most two- and three-syllable words carry 'multiple stress' with a crescendo rising to the final syllable; words without multiple stress carry a single marked stress; words of four or more syllables peak on the second or third syllable and then fall. No fixed stress position is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Multiple stress' on di- and trisyllables: crescendo from the first syllable to the ultimate (bupuwɨ 'blowgun', yábá 'deer'); in words of four or more syllables the crescendo reaches the second or third syllable and then decrescendos (ù'búsé?rò 'fingernail', kapé'wérì 'eyebrow').
new_statements.exceptions: Seven minor pitch patterns of limited membership on trisyllables (p. 19); pitch perturbation with certain possessive pronouns; the suffixes /-a/ 'plural' and /-se/ 'nominalizer' have intrinsic stress and high pitch and perturb the word's pitch pattern (p. 19). The authors say the stress and pitch patterns are 'presented in bare outline' pending fuller analysis (p. 11).

[...] Las palabras monosilábicas que se pronuncian sueltas (no en oraciones o frases) tienen un tono alto. Cuando estas mismas palabras se dicen en una frase u oración, pueden perder el tono alto. new_statements.translation: 3. Tone. Tucano has three tones: high (´), mid (-) and low (`). Only the high tone is marked in the orthography (´). [...] Monosyllabic words pronounced in isolation (not in sentences or phrases) have a high tone. When these same words are said in a phrase or sentence they may lose the high tone. [...] The commonest pattern for two-syllable words is low-high. [p. 18, imperative sentences:] There is one syllable that is emphasized and uttered louder and higher than the rest of the sentence. Generally it is the last or penultimate syllable that is emphasized.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tucano is presented as a tone language with three tones (high, mid, low), only high. monosyllables are high in isolation; commonest disyllabic melody low-high, trisyllables low-mid-high or low-high-low (p. 13); verbs fall into class A (high tone on the last root syllable) and class B (high tone on the first syllable after the root), with the high tone shifting to certain suffixes (pp. 23-24, appendix). The grammar has no section or statement on word stress ('acento' does not occur anywhere in the full-book scanned); the only prominence remark is sentence-level: in imperatives one syllable, usually the last or penultimate of the sentence, is louder and higher.
new_statements.exceptions: Tones change in phrasal context (monosyllables may lose high tone in a sentence); irregular class-A verbs listed in the appendix; high tone moves from root to suffix -a 'remote action' and other suffixes.
new_statements.identity_note: West & Welch 1972 explicitly describes the dialect of Acaricuara on the río Paca (Papurí basin, Vaupés, Colombia), data collected 1963-64, noting vowel differences in other dialects; West 1980 and Welch & West 2004 are Colombian (Vaupés/Papurí) Tucano as used by SIL; none of the opened works concerns Brazilian Tukano (Ramirez's Ye'pâ-masa).

new_statements.quote: 1.3. El tono. Se dan dos tonos en el tucano: el alto ( ´ ) y el bajo ( ` ). En la ortografía, se marca sólo el tono alto (´ ). En los libros que ya se escribieron en tucano, se indican el tono alto solamente en las palabras que, de otro modo, resultarían en una ambigüedad. Es importante aprender los tonos de las palabras en frases completas, porque el contexto muchas veces los modifica [...] [Apéndice I:] Hay dos clases de verbos en cuanto al patrón tonal: A y B. [...] En los verbos de Clase A, el tono alto queda en la última sílaba del radical en todas las formas salvo con el sustantivador -se [...] y el sufijo de tiempo cercano -á [...] En los verbos de Clase B, el tono alto cae en la primera sílaba que sigue al radical.
new_statements.translation: 1.3. Tone. There are two tones in Tucano: high ( ´ ) and low ( ` ). In the orthography only the high tone is marked. In the books already written in Tucano the high tone is indicated only in words that would otherwise be ambiguous. It is important to learn the tones of words in complete sentences, because the context often modifies them [...] [Appendix I:] There are two verb classes as regards tonal pattern: A and B. [...] In Class A verbs the high tone stays on the last syllable of the root in all forms except with the nominalizer -se and the near-tense suffix -á [...] In Class B verbs the high tone falls on the first syllable following the root.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two tones (high/low), only high. minimal pairs by tone (nímá 'poison' vs níma 'they are'); a single high tone whose position is lexical/morphological: verb class A keeps it on the root-final syllable, class B puts it on the first post-root syllable, and it migrates to certain suffixes (plural -a, -se, -á, locatives). Nothing is said about word stress or 'acento' (the string does not occur in the text).
new_statements.exceptions: High tone shifts from root to suffixes -se, -á (class A), always to -a 'remote' in class B; nouns in -ri plural and location nouns lose/shift high tone after demonstratives or with -pʉ/-re (Apéndice VI); context modifies tones in phrases.

new_statements.translation: 5. Suprasegmental phonemes. The suprasegmental features are stress (accent), tone and nasalization. 5.1 Stress. All monosyllabic words are stressed: kí 'bitter manioc', tá 'grass'. Multiple stress appears (1) in two-syllable words, (2) in the two main tone-pattern classes of trisyllabic words, and (3) in various other trisyllables. Stress is marked /'/ in words that do not have multiple stress: pu̥rį 'leaf', diá 'river', pátù 'coca', bi̥pį́rį 'small boards'. In disyllabic and trisyllabic words with multiple stress there is a crescendo from the first syllable to the last [...] 5.2 Tone. The three significant tone levels are: high, mid, low.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule empty, no existing statements; this is the only opened work with an explicit word-stress section: Tucano (Acaricuara dialect) has phonemic stress with lexically varying position plus 'multiple accent', co-existing with three lexical tone levels. Later works by the same authors (0, 1) drop the stress phoneme from the description and keep only tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress ('acento') is listed as a suprasegmental phoneme alongside three contrastive tone levels and nasalization. Monosyllables are always stressed; many di- and trisyllables carry 'multiple accent' (all syllables prominent, realised as a crescendo of intensity from first to last syllable; in words of four or more syllables crescendo to the 2nd or 3rd syllable then decrescendo); in words without multiple accent a single stress is written with /'/ and its position is not predictable from the examples given (initial in pu̥rį 'leaf', pátù 'coca'; final in diá 'river'; medial in bi̥pį́rį). No placement rule is stated; the authors say the multiple-accent and tone patterns await fuller analysis (p. 13) and, in a footnote (p. 21), that the three-tone system seems to be in transition to two tones.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such; instead 'acento múltiple' (several stressed syllables with crescendo, or crescendo-then-decrescendo in words of 4+ syllables); at the phonological-group level a crescendo followed by decrescendo (§9, p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: Low-tone syllables get a strong voiceless off-glide before a stressed syllable beginning with a voiceless consonant (p. 20, §6.1 p. 23); emphatic speech can give a syllable 'exaggerated high tone with heavy stress' (p. 26); tone patterns change with possessive pronouns and with intrinsically high-toned suffixes -a 'plural', -se 'nominalizer' (p. 22).

readall_conflicts: The two sources actually read agree that lexical pitch/tone, not stress position, is the contrastive prosody of Tucano, and neither gives a fixed stress position. They differ in status and analysis: West & Welch 1967 (Acaricuara dialect, Colombia) treat stress as a phonemic suprasegmental with three contrastive pitch levels and nine two/three-syllable pitch patterns, describing 'multiple stress' as a crescendo to the final syllable and single stress marked lexically on other words; Ramirez 1997 (Ye'pâ-masa, Brazil) states flatly that intensity stress has no distinctive function and varies with emphasis (tendency to every-two-moras alternation), and analyses tone as two tonic melodies (high/register vs rising/contour) on bimoraic lexemes plus an atonic low melody, with tone shift onto suffixes and downdrift. So there is a mild disagreement on whether stress is phonemic at all (1967: yes, marked; 1997: no), and a wholesale difference in the tonal analysis (3 levels/pitch patterns vs 2 melodies + atonic), partly attributable to 30 years of analysis and to dialect. The five SIL/Discourse-grammar works could not be opened (dead SIL Colombia URLs, could not be reached by automated download SIL search, the Internet Archive unreachable, lending-only archive.org copy) and one archive.org item was a Cuiva excerpt. No disagreement on stress placement as such, because only one opened work (West & Welch 1972, 'Sistema fonológico del tucano', pp. 20-21) makes a word-stress statement: stre…

sources.quote: 1.3. El tono. Se dan dos tonos en el tucano: el alto ( ´ ) y el bajo ( ` ). En la ortografía, se marca sólo el tono alto (´ ). En los libros que ya se escribieron en tucano, se indican el tono alto solamente en las palabras que, de otro modo, resultarían en una ambigüedad. Es importante aprender los tonos de las palabras en frases completas, porque el contexto muchas veces los modifica [...] [Apéndice I:] Hay dos clases de verbos en cuanto al patrón tonal: A y B. [...] En los verbos de Clase A, el tono alto queda en la última sílaba del radical en todas las formas salvo con el sustantivador -se [...] y el sufijo de tiempo cercano -á [...] En los verbos de Clase B, el tono alto cae en la primera sílaba que sigue al radical.
